subject: Cooking
title: MSG: The Misunderstood Molecule
description: A fast breakdown of MSG: The Misunderstood Molecule for builders.

hook.text: MSG was banned from restaurant menus for decades based on a single anecdotal letter. Not a study — a letter.

buildup.text: In 1968, a doctor wrote to the New England Journal describing headaches after eating Chinese food.

discovery.text: He blamed MSG without evidence. The media amplified it into 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome' — a racist myth.

twist.text: Decades of double-blind studies found no link between MSG and symptoms at normal doses.

climax.text: MSG is just glutamate + sodium — the same glutamate naturally in tomatoes, parmesan, and breast milk.

punchline.text: Science cleared MSG. The stigma just hasn't caught up.

quiz.question: What did scientific studies conclude about MSG causing headaches?
options: Found no link at normal doses
Found it only affects some people

details.summary: Monosodium glutamate is the sodium salt of glutamic acid, a naturally occurring amino acid that triggers umami taste receptors. Despite decades of unfounded fear, rigorous scientific studies consistently find MSG safe at normal culinary doses.
details.whyItMatters: MSG fear is based on debunked research and cultural bias. Understanding MSG's safety and effectiveness lets cooks use one of the most efficient flavor enhancers available.
takeaways: MSG is the sodium salt of naturally occurring glutamic acid
Double-blind studies find no consistent adverse effects at normal doses
MSG adds umami with less sodium than achieving the same depth with salt

faq.question: Is MSG actually safe to eat?
faq.answer: Yes. The FDA classifies MSG as generally recognized as safe. Double-blind, placebo-controlled studies consistently fail to reproduce the symptoms attributed to MSG. The original 1968 letter that sparked fear was anecdotal and has been thoroughly debunked by subsequent research.

faq.question: How should MSG be used in cooking?
faq.answer: Use about half a teaspoon per pound of meat or per four servings. Add it during cooking like salt. It works best in savory dishes — soups, stir-fries, marinades, and sauces. Start with less and adjust. MSG amplifies existing flavors rather than adding a new taste.
